paper_summary: Metal matrix syntactic foams made by inert-gas (Ar) pressure-assisted liquid infiltration of Al99.5, AlSi12, AlMgSi1 and AlCu5 matrices around ceramic hollow spheres (Globocer, 1444 um; SL300, 150 um) at ~64 vol% random close packing were examined after quasi-static (0.01 1/s), split-Hopkinson high strain rate (933 and 2629 1/s) and cyclic compression (R=0.1, f=10 Hz, k=0.7-0.9). Quasi-static loading damages the foam by matrix plasticity with progressive sphere fracture and barrelling, whereas at high strain rate the spheres crack parallel to the load already at ~2.5% strain and fully disintegrate at 2629 1/s, splitting the specimen. Under fatigue the unalloyed Al99.5 matrix foams fail along a single ~45 deg shear band while the harder Si-alloyed AlSi12 foams fail in a lenticular zone between two compression cones, which the authors attribute to the relative yield strength of matrix and ceramic spheres.

processing.particle_grade: Globocer (Hollomet GmbH), 33 wt% Al2O3 / 48 wt% amorphous SiO2 / 19 wt% mullite

structure.microstructure_notes: Random close packed ceramic hollow spheres, ~64 vol%. After 2% engineering deformation the hollow spheres are intact and deformation is carried by matrix plasticity; at 30% the spheres in the specimen centre are broken and the specimen barrels; at 60% the spheres are broken throughout the specimen. No breakage fraction quantified.

test.specimen_notes: Cylindrical D=12.7 mm, H/D=1, MTS 810 hydraulic machine, compressed to 50% engineering strain (sections examined at 2/30/60% deformation); specimens homogenized 520 C / 30 min and water cooled, tested immediately.

evidence.quote: The quasi-static tests were performed on a MTS 810 type hydraulic materials testing machine at room temperature. For the test a 4 column compression tool were used and the tests were made up to 50% engineering deformation with 0.01 s-1 deformation rate.

As filler material two different ceramics hollow spheres were used: Globocer-type made by Hollomet GmbH, and SL300-type made by Envinospheres Ltd. ... The volume fraction of the investigated foams was ~64% due to random close packing (RCP) order
The investigated metal matrix syntactic foams were produced by inert gas (Ar) pressure assisted liquid phase infiltration.

Fig. 2 shows the section of a specimen after 30% engineering deformation in the case of quasi-static compression. It can be seen the hollow spheres which were in the middle of the material are broken. The barrelling of the specimens can be observed as well.

extraction_notes: This is a purely microstructural/fractographic damage study: it reports NO measured mechanical property values (no modulus, strength, plateau stress, energy absorption or fatigue life numbers) in text or tables, so all Properties fields are null and the records carry composition, structure and test-condition metadata only. particle_volume_fraction=0.64 comes from the stated '~64%' random close packing value and applies to all foams. particle_wall_thickness_ratio was computed as eta=(D/2 - t)/(D/2) from Table 2 (Globocer: (722-58)/722=0.92; SL300: (75-6.75)/75=0.91); it is not stated directly in the paper. Engineering deformations quoted in the figures (2%, 2.45%, 8.12%, 10%, 30%, 60%) are the imposed sectioning strains, not strains at failure, so strain_at_failure was left null. Test temperature set to 25 C (quasi-static tests stated 'at room temperature'; the SHPB and fatigue tests are assumed room temperature). Records were created only for the (matrix x filler x test condition) combinations for which results are actually presented. The Materials section also lists AlSi12, AlMgSi1 (O and T6) and AlCu5 (O and T6) matrices with Globocer filler for the monotone compression tests, but the paper states the damage mechanism was 'very similar' and presents no separate data for them, so no records were created for those. Homogenisation 520 C/30 min (and 170 C/14 h T6 ageing for AlMgSi1 and AlCu5) is heat treatment after infiltration; the infiltration temperature is not given, so cure_or_process_temperature_c is null.
